name: NSW English and Mathematics K–6 curriculum skill graph

curriculum.year_placement: Suggested teaching sequence within official stages. Parts A and B are not fixed school-year assignments.
curriculum.status: Original curriculum graph and exercise specifications aligned to the official syllabuses.
curriculum.coverage_note: Every official outcome has mapped nodes. A mapped outcome is not a claim that every content point or authentic performance requirement has been independently demonstrated by the supplied short items.

graph_rules.structure: Directed acyclic graph. Each skill appears exactly once in skills.
graph_rules.children: IDs of skills that directly depend on this skill; look up the matching id in skills.
graph_rules.prerequisites: All listed prerequisites must be met for normal unlocking. A child with several parents does not unlock after only one parent.
graph_rules.diagnostic_entry: Independent placement evidence can demonstrate a target without repeating every earlier node; inferred prerequisite credit is stored separately from directly observed mastery.
graph_rules.review: Review flags are separate from earned mastery and do not create backwards prerequisite edges.
graph_rules.performance_milestones: Collect authentic evidence separately; these never lock ordinary automatic practice.
graph_rules.terminal_nodes: An empty children array marks a node with no direct successor. There are multiple terminal branches, not one artificial end-of-Year-6 gate.

exercise_conventions.type: Interaction type; inspect question, stimulus/audio and options/items for the complete worked example.
exercise_conventions.options: Every selectable option has a stable ID. Answers reference IDs, so shuffling positions does not change correctness.
exercise_conventions.images: A visual_spec or asset brief describes artwork to produce. When it describes choice images, option text names the intended asset for authors; do not display answer-revealing asset labels to students.
exercise_conventions.audio: Production scripts are included; recordings are not. Do not display a dictation or listening transcript during assessment.
exercise_conventions.answers: Choice items use option_id/option_ids. Other interactions use a value, sequence, mapping or explicit rubric according to scoring.type.
exercise_conventions.automatic_scoring: Exact option, set, number, accepted word, ordering, mapping, declared mathematical constraints and explicitly specified geometry checks are deterministic design specifications. They still require a renderer and checking implementation.
exercise_conventions.rubrics: An open-performance rubric is not a deterministic answer key. Automated assistance and exception review may collect evidence without claiming that a quiz proves the entire performance.
exercise_conventions.variation: Each skill has at least two worked exercise templates. Follow variation_rules to author or validate independent items, with complete required subfamily coverage.
exercise_conventions.practice_items: Concrete new items live in skills[].practice_items. The original exercises remain worked authoring examples; each has practice_item_ids linking to the new items. Deliver the new items to learners.
exercise_conventions.feedback_timing: New-item explanations and answer keys are author-only until a response is submitted.

automatic_practice.required_skills: All skills where assessment_mode is automatic
automatic_practice.completion_evidence: Secure mastery or separately recorded diagnostic credit
automatic_practice.meaning: The automatically checked practice graph is complete; this alone does not establish every performance outcome.

full_program.completion_evidence: Independent micro-skill mastery, sufficient authentic performance evidence, and the whole_program_requirements ledger
full_program.meaning: All parts of this curriculum design have evidence. This is not automatic official certification.

skills.name: Share objects fairly into equal groups
skills.subject: maths
skills.description: Independently share objects fairly into equal groups, using a new example and checking the result.

exercises.question: Share six crackers equally onto two plates. How many on each?
exercises.variation_rules: Use2–4 groups and totals≤12 that divide evenly; one-at-a-time sharing.
exercises.misconception_feedback: Equal groups means each recipient gets at least one.

additional_design.assessment_note: Worked authoring examples. They do not themselves constitute a complete calibrated item bank; generate new instances under the stated variation constraints and verify each answer.

exercises.question: Which sharing is fair for eight counters on two mats?
exercises.variation_rules: Use2–4 groups and totals≤12 that divide evenly; one-at-a-time sharing.
exercises.misconception_feedback: Equal groups means each recipient gets at least one.

additional_design.assessment_note: Worked authoring examples. They do not themselves constitute a complete calibrated item bank; generate new instances under the stated variation constraints and verify each answer.

exercises.question: Share all six counters fairly between the two mats. Leave your counters on the mats to show your answer.

stimulus.presentation_note: Use two equally sized mats. Tokens carry hidden stable IDs but are visually identical. Each token can be placed once; it cannot be duplicated.

exercises.variation_rules: Use small divisible totals and two or three mats. Accept every token arrangement satisfying the count constraints; do not require particular token IDs on particular mats. Separate sharing a total from making groups of a specified size.
exercises.misconception_feedback: The learner may divide the counters into unequal groups, leave some in the tray or count the same counter twice.

additional_design.assessment_note: The completed arrangement is the learner's constructed grouping record. The automatic check scores the mathematical structure, not a prescribed drag order.

common_misconceptions: Equal groups means each recipient gets at least one.

exercises.question: A clap lasts one second. A song lasts two minutes. Which takes longer?
exercises.variation_rules: Use paired animation timers with common starts; seconds/minutes supplied by narration.

skills.description: Independently answer a question to contribute to data, using a new example and checking the result.

exercises.question: The question is Which fruit do you prefer? Which is a suitable answer?
exercises.variation_rules: Use familiar categorical questions and one clearly defined response per participant.
exercises.misconception_feedback: One response can be counted multiple times.

additional_design.assessment_note: Worked authoring examples. They do not themselves constitute a complete calibrated item bank; generate new instances under the stated variation constraints and verify each answer.

exercises.question: Which result cannot be known for certain before acting?

stimulus.model_assumptions: Where a random model is used: mix well; each physical counter is equally likely; named fair dice/coins have equally likely faces; spinner sectors are drawn to their specified angles. Replacement occurs only when stated.

exercises.question: Two cubes make this rectangular prism. Draw its visible outside edges on the dot grid in the same view. Start at the marked top corner. Leave out hidden edges and the seam between the cubes.

scoring.orientation_reason: The question explicitly requests the displayed view and provides a fixed top-corner anchor.

render_transform.purpose: The integer logical grid becomes a true equal-axis isometric projection on screen. Scoring uses the original snapped logical coordinates.

stimulus.drawing_tool: join two grid dots with a straight edge
stimulus.presentation_note: Render the model and response grid at the same orientation and scale. Use the supplied projection to draw the model; do not use perspective or a generated approximate illustration. The anchor fixes translation.

exercises.variation_rules: Supply fresh connected-cube models and different specified views with independently verified projections. Also include top/front/side outline drawings and constructing a model from a drawing. Where orientation is not fixed by the question, accept all geometrically equivalent rotations.
exercises.misconception_feedback: A flat rectangle omits depth; an incorrect receding edge changes the shown view; adding hidden edges does not follow the requested visible-edge convention.

additional_design.assessment_note: Original isometric sketch specification with a checked visible-edge set. It provides actual student construction rather than choosing a finished drawing; other prism/pyramid and view variants remain item-family authoring requirements.

skills.name: Recognise letter orientation and starting points
skills.subject: english
skills.description: Identify modelled letter shapes and formation paths. This is preparation for handwriting, not evidence of independent pen control.

exercises.question: Which is b?

stimulus.asset_brief: Art brief: correct b and mirror-reversed b, labelled A and B.

exercises.variation_rules: Generate unfamiliar examples of recognise letter orientation and starting points. Keep the assessed feature and taught code constant; change names, content words and correct-answer position. Review that exactly the keyed answer fits the supplied context.
exercises.misconception_feedback: Distractors change the target recognise letter orientation and starting points feature while retaining plausible surface wording; identify the selected error before giving a hint.

skills.evidence_limits: Correct structured responses demonstrate this target only; sustained speaking, oral reading, handwriting and original composition have separate performance checkpoints.

stimulus.text:
The missing wheel

Mina laid the model car on the table. One wheel was missing, and the race would begin after lunch. She searched her bag, then checked beneath the chairs. Nothing.

"You can borrow mine," said Theo, holding up a spare. Mina almost accepted, but the wheel was much larger than the other three. She rolled the model gently and watched it tilt. Together they opened the class box of spare parts. At the bottom lay a wheel of the right size.

Mina fitted it, tested the axle and smiled. The search had taken time, but now she knew the model would roll evenly.

The dry patch

Across the creek

The stepping stones were usually easy to cross. Today, water curled around their tops. Ava lifted one foot towards the first stone, then stopped.

"We crossed here last week," said her brother. Ava pointed to a twig racing past. The water was moving much faster now. She unfolded the map and found a footbridge farther upstream.

The class library had three crowded shelves. Pupils often returned books wherever they found a gap, and familiar titles became hard to locate.

The quiet rehearsal

The choir could sing every word of the song, but the ending sounded untidy. Some singers held the final note while others stopped early.

At the next run-through, the final note stopped together. The change was small, but the whole song sounded more confident. Knowing the words had been one part of the task; listening to one another was another.

A borrowed telescope

The science club borrowed a telescope for an evening display. Before touching it, the pupils read the supplied instructions and checked the stand. They chose a clear viewing area away from bright lights.

Clouds covered the sky just as the families arrived. Instead of pretending the view was clear, the club explained the problem and showed a labelled model of the equipment. Visitors asked how the lenses worked.

Later, a gap appeared between the clouds. The pupils used the opportunity carefully, while those waiting continued discussing the model.

The small donation

At the book collection, most people carried large bags. Eli arrived with one thin book, wrapped in paper. He hesitated beside the table.

The organiser opened it and read the title. "We have been looking for a copy of this," she said. A younger reader had requested the story, but every copy was on loan.

The changed timetable

A notice announced that the afternoon bus would leave ten minutes earlier on Friday. Leila copied the time into her planner, then told her friends.

One friend remembered an older notice with a different time. They checked the dates together and found that the new notice replaced the old one. Leila asked the office to confirm the change before their class passed on the message.

On Friday, everyone arrived at the stop early enough. Remembering a time was useful, but checking which notice was current had mattered more.

The pond is open, but the track is closed.

practice_items.question: Which origin note stays within this evidence?

options.text: Kangaroo: from Guugu Yimidhirr; credit this ANU source.
Kangaroo: the original word in every Aboriginal language.
Kangaroo: a word invented by Cook without a source language.

practice_items.explanation: The evidence names one language and place. It does not establish a word shared by every Aboriginal language.

stimulus.text:
Paraphrased source note: English kangaroo was borrowed from Guugu Yimidhirr near Cooktown. The recorded word named a particular large kangaroo.

practice_items.question: Read the entire passage aloud independently. Then answer: Why could the class not conclude that lower bridges are always stronger?
practice_items.target: The trial that surprised us

stimulus.text:
The trial that surprised us

Our class predicted that a taller paper bridge would carry more weight. We built two designs from the same amount of card and tested them over the same gap. To our surprise, the lower bridge held more washers.

At first, the designers argued that the test must be wrong. Then we examined the folded supports. The lower bridge had a wider base, while the taller bridge’s legs bent sideways. Height was not the only feature that had changed.

We recorded the result, including the unexpected failure. For the next test, we planned to keep the support shape the same and vary only height. The first trial had not answered our original question cleanly, but it had shown us how to ask it more carefully.

answer.exemplar: The designs differed in support shape as well as height, and only this limited test was performed.
answer.acceptable_variation: Any original response that meets the task and rubric; the exemplar is not a unique correct answer.

practice_items.target: The map in the drawer

stimulus.text:
The map in the drawer

When the old community hall was renovated, an unlabelled map appeared in a desk drawer. Its creek ran where a car park now stood. Rosa wanted to display it as proof that the creek had been filled in.

Her grandfather pointed to the missing date. The map might have been a plan rather than a record. They compared it with dated photographs and council documents, finding that a channel had once crossed part of the site.

The display eventually described both the evidence and the remaining uncertainty. Rosa liked the mystery less once it became a careful explanation, but she trusted the explanation more. Visitors could now see what was known and what was still being investigated.

practice_items.question: Read the entire passage aloud independently. Then answer: What does Lila’s choice reveal about her values?
practice_items.target: The captain’s pause

stimulus.text:
The captain’s pause

The coach praised the captain for the team’s rescue of a failing project. Applause began, and Lila stepped towards the microphone. In her pocket was the note showing who had actually solved the wiring problem.

She could have accepted the simple story. Instead, she named the quiet teammate who had stayed late to test each connection. Then she described the people who had built the frame, checked the instructions and recorded the results.

The applause became less tidy as names were called and hands waved across the room. Lila paused until the noise settled. The story took longer to tell that way, but it was closer to the truth.

answer.exemplar: She values accurate recognition and shared contribution over taking all the credit.

practice_items.target: A proposal with a price

stimulus.text:
A proposal with a price

A new covered area could keep pupils dry at lunchtime. In a survey, most respondents supported it, but several worried that the structure would remove a favourite patch of grass. The design team first treated those comments as obstacles.

After visiting the site, they understood the concern. The grass was the only nearby space used for quiet outdoor games. They revised the design to cover an existing paved section instead. This option cost more, so they proposed a smaller trial structure and a review of its use.

Their final recommendation was less dramatic than the first drawing. It also answered more of the questions that mattered to the people who would use it.

answer.exemplar: It revealed a valued use of the grass and led to a revised, qualified plan that addressed the trade-off.

practice_items.question: Read the entire passage aloud independently. Then answer: Why did Sam qualify the article’s opening claim?
practice_items.target: The last paragraph

stimulus.text:
The last paragraph

The article began with an exciting claim: a new method had transformed reading in a single week. Sam nearly copied the sentence into his report. Then he reached the final paragraph.

Only twelve volunteers had taken part, all from the same club. The article reported their comments but no independent assessment of improvement. Some participants enjoyed the method, while two had stopped early.

Sam rewrote his note. The small trial suggested that several volunteers liked the activity; it did not show that every learner would improve. His sentence sounded less impressive, but it preserved the evidence. The final paragraph had changed how he understood the first.

answer.exemplar: The small self-selected sample, subjective reports and withdrawals did not support a universal claim of improvement.

practice_items.target: The lantern on the shelf

stimulus.text:
The lantern on the shelf

For years, the lantern had stood unused beside the window. Mara’s grandfather cleaned it each winter, although the house had electric lights. He said little about the practice.

During a long power failure, neighbours gathered in their kitchen. The lantern lit the table while people shared food, news and spare batteries. Mara noticed that her grandfather placed it in the centre, where everyone could see.

After the lights returned, she asked why he kept it. He described nights when a neighbour’s small light had helped his own family feel less alone. Mara put the lantern back carefully. It was still an old object, but it now carried a history of welcome.

answer.exemplar: It shifts from an unexplained old object to a symbol of shared help and welcome, supported by the present gathering and past account.

practice_items.question: Read the entire passage aloud independently. Then answer: What distinction does the class make between the result and its cause?
practice_items.target: An uneven result

stimulus.text:
An uneven result

The class tested two versions of a sign. Ten visitors followed the large-print version correctly, while seven followed the smaller one. The group was ready to recommend large print everywhere.

A second look at the records complicated the result. The large-print sign also had a clear arrow, and it had been placed closer to the entrance. The smaller sign used neither feature. The test showed that one complete design worked better in those conditions, but it did not isolate the effect of print size.

The pupils kept the useful result and changed the next experiment. They would compare signs with the same arrow and position, varying only the size of the lettering.

answer.exemplar: One complete design performed better, but several changed features prevent attributing the difference solely to print size.

practice_items.target: The invitation

stimulus.text:
The invitation

When the town announced a public mural, Isaac imagined a row of brilliant pictures painted by experts. At the first meeting, the organisers placed blank cards on every table. They asked residents what the wall should say about the place.

A shopkeeper described early deliveries. A child drew the creek after rain. An older resident remembered a tree that no longer stood. Their ideas did not form one simple image, and the first discussion ended without a design.

Isaac thought the meeting had failed until he saw the artist grouping the cards by shared themes. The wall, he realised, needed a careful conversation before it needed paint.

answer.exemplar: He sees that gathering different perspectives is useful preparation for a meaningful design, even without an immediate finished image.

practice_items.question: Read the entire passage aloud independently. Then answer: Why is successful alone an incomplete description?
practice_items.target: A quieter machine

stimulus.text:
A quieter machine

The makers’ club built a small sorting machine. It worked quickly, but its rattling interrupted nearby readers. Some members argued that speed mattered most. Others suggested abandoning the machine entirely.

The group tested pads under the base and replaced a loose wheel. The machine became quieter, although it sorted a little more slowly. They recorded both changes and asked the readers whether the remaining noise was acceptable.

The revised design did not maximise every measure. It balanced a useful function with the needs of the shared space. Their report described the compromise rather than hiding it behind the single word successful.

answer.exemplar: The design improved noise but lost some speed, so the conclusion needs to explain the trade-off and the users’ needs.

practice_items.question: Read the entire passage aloud independently. Then answer: How can the two accounts differ without either automatically being false?
practice_items.target: The second voice

stimulus.text:
The second voice

The travel diary described the market as chaotic. Its author had arrived hurriedly, missed the entrance sign and misunderstood the queue. A later interview with a stallholder described the same morning differently.

The stallholder explained how deliveries were arranged before the stalls opened and how regular customers knew where to wait. Neither account could be treated as a view from nowhere. The visitor noticed confusion; the stallholder noticed familiar routines.

In her comparison, Talia kept both perspectives. She did not pretend that one person’s experience cancelled the other’s. Instead, she explained how position, knowledge and purpose affected what each account made visible.

answer.exemplar: They describe the event from different roles and levels of familiarity; each perspective highlights different experiences.

stimulus.text:
Text A — original story account: Ari found a wallet beside the gate. He wanted to hurry home, but he took it to the office and waited to explain where it had been.
Text B — original account from another participant: Ari’s friend said, "I first thought he was wasting time because we needed to get home. After he explained that the wallet could contain someone’s important belongings, I understood why he went to the office."
Comparison question: Compare how the two accounts judge Ari’s delay. What information explains the friend’s change of view?
Discuss with a partner. Each person should compare evidence from both texts, accurately paraphrase the other person’s view and negotiate a shared conclusion or a clearly stated disagreement.

assessment_policy.status: Proposed product rules to calibrate with students; these thresholds are not NESA requirements.
principles: A node represents one assessable skill, not one fixed question or one entire syllabus outcome.
Hard prerequisite edges are acyclic. Revision is a scheduler action and never a backward prerequisite edge.
School year is a suggested teaching placement. NSW stage outcomes and the syllabus content remain authoritative.
Most English practice uses exact, finite-answer checks. Open speaking, handwriting and original composition require additional performance evidence.
Performance milestones do not block ordinary automatically checked practice. Completing practice alone does not establish every syllabus outcome.
An incorrect answer triggers specific feedback and a new example, without removing earned progress in unrelated branches.
An item may teach more than one idea, but an assessment response is credited only to the skill it actually isolates.

unlock_rule.all_of: Every ID in prerequisites has earned provisional or secure mastery, unless the learner demonstrates the target directly through a placement assessment. A review_due flag does not remove earned prerequisite credit or relock descendants.
unlock_rule.soft_prerequisites: Recommended support only. They do not lock the node.
unlock_rule.placement: Use unseen target questions across representations to place an experienced student. Mark skipped ancestors as inferred, not directly observed mastery. Recheck them only when target performance exposes a gap.
unlock_rule.performance: No auto-checkable micro-skill needs an adult-reviewed performance node as a hard prerequisite.

mastery_rule.practice: Instruction, worked examples and hints are available freely. Hint-assisted responses never count as independent mastery evidence.

provisional.systematic_error_rule: No unresolved repeated critical misconception in the most recent checks.
provisional.parameter_coverage_rule: Cover every required subfamily named in the node over the accumulated independent evidence history. The recent ten items are an additional stability window, not the total evidence limit. Nodes covering all graphemes or many spelling patterns need more than ten total items. A few easy examples cannot stand for all graphemes, regrouping cases, text purposes or representations.
provisional.scope: These are initial design values. Calibrate difficulty, reliability and burden with learner data. Do not convert them into an IXL SmartScore.

mastery_rule.secure: Pass two new, unassisted mixed-review items on a later day, initially scheduled around seven days after provisional mastery.
mastery_rule.maintenance: Revisit around 28 days and in later integrated tasks. A failed review opens targeted practice; it does not erase previously mastered downstream work.
mastery_rule.timing: Response speed is diagnostic only unless fluency is the declared construct. Never impose a countdown on ordinary learning.
mastery_rule.low_burden: Split evidence over short sessions. A learner is never required to complete all ten checks in one sitting.

session_design.performance: Short recordings, writing chunks and practical demonstrations may take longer. The complete text or presentation can be assembled over sessions.
session_design.selection: Prefer available nodes that resolve a demonstrated gap or unlock several appropriate next skills. Offer a choice between strands without demanding completion of an entire year.

assessment_routes.auto_exact: Deterministic answer key, accepted equivalent values, sets, sequences, mappings or constrained edits. Suitable for most micro-skills.
assessment_routes.automated_assisted: Speech alignment, handwriting or writing feedback can collect and organise evidence. Confidence and rubric results must be visible. These models are not implemented or validated by this design.
assessment_routes.exception_review: Ask an adult only when a production judgement remains ambiguous, the learner disputes it, or an outcome requires authentic observation. Use selected milestone samples rather than reviewing every practice response.
assessment_routes.adult_observation: Sustained discussion, handwriting movement or physical measurement may need an observed performance. Clicking a correct example is preparation, not evidence of performing that skill.

scoring_conventions.numbers: Parse signed integers, decimals and fractions exactly where possible. Declare required units and rounding. Accept equivalent fractions unless simplest form is the skill.
scoring_conventions.money: Use Australian dollars and cents; store canonical values as integer cents. Teach distinct coin denomination from physical size.
scoring_conventions.spelling: Use Australian English. Disable autocomplete, spelling correction and predictive suggestions when spelling is being assessed. Ignore outer whitespace but not target letters.
scoring_conventions.punctuation: Preserve the punctuation feature under test. Declare accepted straight/curly apostrophe and quote equivalents.
scoring_conventions.case: Ignore case only where capitals are not the assessment target.
scoring_conventions.ordering: Support all valid sequences or design the context to make a unique sequence. Do not reject a grammatically valid alternative merely because it differs from the exemplar.
scoring_conventions.multi_select: Feedback may identify partially correct choices; independent mastery requires the complete correct set and no incorrect additions.
scoring_conventions.reading: Do not use read-aloud of the target passage as evidence of independent reading comprehension. Record listening comprehension separately.
scoring_conventions.dictation: Audio text is an authoring transcript only, hidden from the student. Replay is allowed. Do not show the target word in captions, file names, alt text or feedback before submission.
scoring_conventions.speech: Do not treat speech-recognition transcription as perfect evidence of phoneme accuracy, accent, prosody or communication quality.
scoring_conventions.images: Use an accessible equivalent task where visual access changes the construct. Do not put the answer in alt text. Use measured geometry for shapes, not ambiguous generated art.

accessibility: Touch targets at least 44 CSS pixels with adequate spacing; keyboard alternatives for every action.
Tap-to-select followed by tap-to-place is available for ordering, matching and number lines. Dragging is optional.
Audio instructions for early learners; mathematics progress is not gated by English decoding.
Use labels, shapes and text as well as colour. Allow magnification, switch access and reduced motion.
AAC, Auslan and other communication adjustments follow the learner's access needs. Record the construct and mode so support is not mistaken for independent decoding.
Keep mathematics quantities perceptually clear. Vary arrangement and object size without adding irrelevant counting ambiguity.

content_generation.authority: The graph, answer logic, number bounds, taught phonics and item validation rules are fixed curriculum data.
content_generation.generative_role: A generative model may provide story contexts, approved text variants and feedback. It must not invent prerequisites, change the target skill, or decide exact answers independently.
content_generation.validation: Validate every generated item for a unique answer or explicit accepted alternatives, age-appropriate wording, correct mathematics, decodability when relevant, and absence of answer leaks.
content_generation.bank_minimum: Before production, author or validate enough independent variants to meet the mastery and delayed-review rules; the two supplied templates per node are worked specifications, not a finished item bank.

interaction_types.label: Choose one
interaction_types.student_action: Tap one picture, word, sentence or answer.
interaction_types.marking: Compare a stable option ID, not the displayed position.
interaction_types.use: Shape recognition; sound-letter match; main idea; inference; grammatical choice.
interaction_types.design_rule: Vary option order, keep distractors plausible, and ensure only one best answer under the stated question.

interaction_types.label: Choose all that apply
interaction_types.student_action: Tap every matching answer, then submit.
interaction_types.marking: Compare the selected set with the complete accepted set.
interaction_types.use: Properties of shapes; evidence sentences; plural endings; equivalent fractions.
interaction_types.design_rule: Make the instruction explicit and include examples with more than one correct choice.

interaction_types.label: Enter a number
interaction_types.student_action: Use a numeric keypad, fraction editor or short numeric field.
interaction_types.marking: Exact rational/numeric comparison, with required precision and units declared.
interaction_types.use: Counting; operations; missing values; measurement; probability.
interaction_types.design_rule: Avoid a choice-only bank that can be completed by guessing; accept mathematically equivalent answers when appropriate.

interaction_types.label: Type a word
interaction_types.student_action: Type a missing word, spelling, inflection or short response.
interaction_types.marking: An explicit accepted-answer list with construct-sensitive normalisation.
interaction_types.use: Spelling from audio; morphology; grammar gaps; vocabulary in context.
interaction_types.design_rule: Use a sentence/audio context to disambiguate homophones; suppress predictive text when it would supply the target.

interaction_types.label: Put in order
interaction_types.student_action: Tap items in order or move tiles using pointer or keyboard.
interaction_types.marking: Accepted sequence or a constraint checker for multiple valid orders.
interaction_types.use: Numerals; story events; sentence building; paragraph structure; steps in reasoning.
interaction_types.design_rule: Start from a genuinely shuffled display. Allow selecting and moving without dragging.

interaction_types.label: Match pairs
interaction_types.student_action: Select an item and then its partner.
interaction_types.marking: Compare a mapping of item IDs.
interaction_types.use: Words and definitions; fractions and pictures; shapes and nets; causes and effects.
interaction_types.design_rule: Do not let line-crossing, colour or position reveal the mapping.

interaction_types.label: Sort into groups
interaction_types.student_action: Tap an item, then its group.
interaction_types.marking: Compare item-to-category assignments; declare whether categories overlap.
interaction_types.use: Phonemes; text purposes; nouns/verbs; shape classes; data types.
interaction_types.design_rule: Use inclusive mathematical definitions: a square can also be a rectangle, unless mutually exclusive categories are deliberately defined.

interaction_types.label: Place on a line
interaction_types.student_action: Tap a tick or use an accessible value selector.
interaction_types.marking: Compare the intended value, not raw pixel coordinates.
interaction_types.use: Whole numbers; fractions; decimals; signed integers; probability scale.
interaction_types.design_rule: Tick scale, endpoints and snapping rules must be explicit.

interaction_types.label: Edit or write briefly
interaction_types.student_action: Correct a sentence or produce a bounded response.
interaction_types.marking: Use deterministic constrained edits where possible; a rubric for genuinely open responses.
interaction_types.use: Capitalisation; punctuation; sentence combining; summaries; original composition.
interaction_types.design_rule: Do not treat one model sentence as the only correct answer to an open writing task.

interaction_types.label: Read or speak
interaction_types.student_action: Record a short reading, explanation or presentation.
interaction_types.marking: Align expected words where appropriate; assess meaning/prosody through a separate rubric and confidence-aware review.
interaction_types.use: Fluency; oral storytelling; mathematical explanation; communication.
interaction_types.design_rule: Speech-to-text accuracy alone cannot establish the full outcome; allow communication alternatives.

interaction_types.label: Draw or write
interaction_types.student_action: Use a finger/stylus or a paper sample.
interaction_types.marking: Geometry rules can check some drawings. Handwriting quality and movement require additional evidence.
interaction_types.use: Letter formation; shapes; nets; measurement diagrams.
interaction_types.design_rule: Provide motor-access alternatives and avoid marking finger precision as conceptual understanding.

interaction_types.label: Apply the skill
interaction_types.student_action: Complete a brief practical, discussion, reading or composition task.
interaction_types.marking: Collect a work sample against a small explicit rubric, with automated assistance and exception review where appropriate.
interaction_types.use: Authentic English production; physical measurement; sustained communication; integrated transfer.
interaction_types.design_rule: Keep these as separate evidence milestones, with ordinary micro-skill practice available independently.

practice_bank.status: Authored and structurally validated; learner calibration and application integration are separate.
practice_bank.content_provenance: Questions, passages, distractors and feedback are authored for this bank. Numerical families are deterministically parameterised. Where supplied cultural context or etymology relies on a public source, per-item source URLs and qualifications are retained. Existing curriculum mappings are inherited, not independently recertified.

delivery_contract.learner_payload: Build a dedicated learner payload; never send the full authoring graph to the learner client. Deliver the question, permitted stimulus/media, shuffled selectable content, input controls and necessary instructions only.
delivery_contract.hidden_media: Audio scripts, phoneme production directions, tone/delivery labels, option author labels and answer-bearing geometry specifications are for the renderer/producer only. Render the intended audio, image or interaction; do not print these metadata as stimulus text.
delivery_contract.audio: Scripts are complete but recordings are not included. Record or synthesise en-AU audio, then review phonemes, pronunciation and expressive delivery. hide_transcript=true is mandatory during listening or dictation. Honour read_target_aloud=false and option_audio_allowed=false. Reading and listening evidence must be tracked separately.
delivery_contract.visuals: Inline SVGs can be rendered directly. Structured visual_spec, maps, clocks, calendars, tables, rulers and geometry objects need a faithful renderer. Supply keyboard and touch alternatives, and do not expose correct answers in alt text.
delivery_contract.feedback: Show explanation only after submission. Retain the selected response to identify the actual misconception; explanations are general correct-answer feedback, not a claim that every distractor has a separately authored diagnostic message.
delivery_contract.performance: Rubrics describe observable evidence and acceptable variation. They are not unique answer keys. Collect authentic work and use confidence-aware human/teacher review where required by the original assessment policy.
delivery_contract.time: estimated_seconds is guidance, not a countdown or a mastery criterion.
delivery_contract.eligibility: Apply taught-grapheme eligibility and assessment_facet/coverage_tags where supplied. Reading and spelling demonstrations are separate evidence facets even when a node combines them.

scoring_contract.exact_option: Compare response option ID with correct_option_id, independently of display order.
scoring_contract.exact_set: Require all and only correct_option_ids; order is irrelevant.
scoring_contract.numeric: Parse exact rational values. Enforce the declared input formats, unit, tolerance and format_constraints first. accept_equivalent_fractions never overrides an explicit notation constraint. Decimal-place requirements need the original input string. canonical_cents is the exact money amount in cents when present.
scoring_contract.exact: Apply only the item-declared normalisation, then compare with accepted strings. Preserve target capitals, letters and punctuation. A missing optional normalisation flag is false.
scoring_contract.sequence: Accept any sequence in accepted_sequences. Stable item IDs distinguish tiles even when text repeats.
scoring_contract.mapping: Accept mapping or any declared accepted_mappings. Compare item-to-category/partner IDs, not screen positions.
scoring_contract.constraints: Use every declared item ID exactly once, use only allowed categories, and satisfy group_counts. Do not constrain equivalent individual objects to one arbitrary assignment.
scoring_contract.geometry: Implement the explicit coordinate, edge, point, angle, tolerance and exact-cover predicates. These are checking specifications, not an included geometry engine.
scoring_contract.rubric: Score each criterion 0, 1 or 2 from observed evidence. max_score is the sum of criterion maxima. requires_review=true and automatic=false must remain in force.

selection_contract.purpose: practice, transfer_check and review are intended uses, not proof of unseen exposure or calibrated difficulty.
selection_contract.difficulty: support, core and stretch are authoring judgements; calibrate with learner responses.
selection_contract.novelty: Track item IDs and stimulus_group_id across skills. Repeated exposure to the same passage/audio/visual is not an unseen transfer item merely because its question differs. Fingerprints identify identical supplied objects, not all semantic overlap.
selection_contract.mastery: Retain the original multi-session mastery and required-subfamily coverage rules. The ten-item minimum is a bank-size floor, not a guarantee that a learner can satisfy every mastery criterion from only ten attempted items. Expand/replenish the finite bank when unseen items are exhausted.

evidence_limits: Structural checks and declared-key consistency do not prove every linguistic judgement or distractor is valid.
Numerical subsets were independently recalculated; all conceptual items have not been empirically tested with pupils.
The graph maps syllabus outcomes and content groups but does not certify complete content-point coverage.
Text-based artwork tasks interpret the supplied attributed description; they do not reproduce an artwork or establish independent visual analysis of an unseen work.
Public cultural descriptions and dictionary entries are scoped to their named communities, languages and sources; they do not grant permission for unrelated or restricted cultural uses.

unresolved_source_dependent_facets.detail: The generic map-and-key skill has ten concrete items. A culturally authorised source map with its actual legend is not reproduced in this bank. This specific source-dependent variation remains to be supplied before claiming full variation-rule coverage.

visual_asset_policy.preferred_icon_source: Font Awesome Free Solid SVG icons
visual_asset_policy.icon_policy: Icons are useful for concrete countable objects, story contexts, category labels and map landmarks. Avoid generic icon substitution for exact geometric figures, clocks, measurement scales, phonics and spelling.
visual_asset_policy.implementation: Use @fortawesome/react-fontawesome and individually imported icons from @fortawesome/free-solid-svg-icons; pin the version, maintain a validated allowlist and tree-shake.
visual_asset_policy.license: Font Awesome Free SVG/JS icons: CC BY 4.0; retain required attribution and licence notices.
visual_qa: No answer-revealing images or alt text

visual_enhancement_summary.note: Suggestions are authoring metadata, not generated assets or verified icon imports.
